muhammad-bin-hasan-al-baghdadi.name: al-Baghdadi
muhammad-bin-hasan-al-baghdadi.summary: Compiler of an early Abbasid-era Arab cookbook, Kitab al-Tabikh, written in 1226 with 160 recipes, who died in 1239.

dolma.name: Dolma
dolma.summary: A family of stuffed dishes, mainly vegetables or leaves filled with rice, meat and spices, associated with Ottoman cuisine and spread across former Ottoman regions.

masgouf.name: Masgouf
masgouf.summary: A Mesopotamian dish of seasoned, grilled carp, often considered the national dish of Iraq.

krak-des-chevaliers.name: Krak des Chevaliers
krak-des-chevaliers.summary: Medieval castle in Syria given to the Knights Hospitaller in 1142 and later rebuilt into a concentric fortress; at its peak it housed a garrison of about 2,000.

knights-hospitaller.name: Knights Hospitaller
knights-hospitaller.summary: A Catholic military order founded in 12th-century crusader Jerusalem to care for and defend pilgrims, later based in Cyprus, Rhodes, Malta and Saint Petersburg.

great-mosque-of-aleppo.name: Great Mosque of Aleppo
great-mosque-of-aleppo.summary: The largest and one of the oldest mosques in Aleppo, Syria, first built in the early 8th century under the Umayyads, with its current structure dating from the 11th to 14th centuries.

ibn-al-khashshab.name: Ibn al-Khashshab
ibn-al-khashshab.summary: Muslim judge and civic leader (rais) of Aleppo, who served under the Seljuk emir Ridwan and died in 1125.

hejaz.name: Hejaz
hejaz.summary: A historical region of western Arabia, in modern Saudi Arabia, containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, the first and second holiest sites in Islam.

madrasa.name: Madrasa
madrasa.summary: Arabic word for a school of any kind, which in the historic Muslim world usually meant an institution teaching Islamic law, spreading widely after being pioneered by the vizier Nizam al-Mulk in the 11th century.

concentric-castle.name: Concentric castle
concentric-castle.summary: A castle design with two or more nested curtain walls, the outer lower than the inner so it can be defended from within, typically built without a central keep.

mirdasid-dynasty.name: Mirdasid dynasty
mirdasid-dynasty.summary: An Arab Shia Muslim dynasty that ruled an Aleppo-based emirate in northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia from 1014 to 1080.

zengid-dynasty.name: Zengid dynasty
zengid-dynasty.summary: A Turkoman Sunni Muslim dynasty founded in 1127 that ruled the Levant and Upper Mesopotamia, seized Fatimid Egypt in 1169, and became renowned for fighting the Crusaders.

between-the-crusades-1149-1189.name: Nur al-Din
between-the-crusades-1149-1189.summary: Zengid ruler who succeeded his father Zengi and built a Syrian-Egyptian alliance against the Crusader states, later completed when Saladin became sultan of Egypt and Syria.

qalawun.name: Qalawun
qalawun.summary: Seventh Bahri Mamluk sultan of Egypt, ruling from 1279 to 1290, who founded the Qalawunid dynasty and waged war against the Crusaders, capturing their territory.

caravanserai.name: Caravanserai
caravanserai.summary: A roadside or urban inn common across the Islamic world that sheltered travelers, merchants and pack animals along trade routes such as the Silk Road.

saladin.name: Saladin
saladin.summary: Founder of the Ayyubid dynasty and first sultan of Egypt and Syria (c. 1137 to 1193), who led the Muslim military effort against the Crusader states during the Third Crusade.

al-zahir-ghazi.name: Al-Zahir Ghazi
al-zahir-ghazi.summary: Kurdish Ayyubid emir of Aleppo from 1186 to 1216 and the third son of Saladin, ruling northern Syria and part of Mesopotamia.

citadel-of-aleppo.name: Citadel of Aleppo
citadel-of-aleppo.summary: A large medieval fortified palace in Aleppo, Syria, among the oldest and largest castles in the world, mostly dating from the Ayyubid period.

minbar.name: Minbar
minbar.summary: A pulpit in a mosque from which the imam delivers sermons, also used in similar settings such as a Husayniyya.

mihrab.name: Mihrab
mihrab.summary: A niche in a mosque's wall marking the qibla, the direction of Mecca, toward which Muslims face when praying.

al-nasir-muhammad.name: al-Nasir Muhammad
al-nasir-muhammad.summary: Ninth Mamluk sultan of the Bahri dynasty, ruling Egypt across three reigns between 1293 and 1341, who reformed taxation and appointed loyal officials to fight corruption.

al-ashraf-khalil.name: Al-Ashraf Khalil
al-ashraf-khalil.summary: Eighth Bahri Mamluk sultan of Egypt (1290-1293), famed for capturing Acre in 1291 and ending the last Crusader state in Palestine, before being assassinated.

mansouri-great-mosque.name: Great Mosque of Tripoli
mansouri-great-mosque.summary: A mosque in Tripoli, Lebanon, built by the Mamluks between 1294 and 1298 on the site of an earlier Crusader church, the first building erected in Mamluk Tripoli.

kufic.name: Kufic script
kufic.summary: Angular, early style of Arabic script that developed in the city of Kufa, prized for Quran transcription and architectural decoration.

naskh-script.name: Naskh script
naskh-script.summary: A small, round style of Islamic calligraphy, among the earliest to develop, widely used for administrative documents and for copying books, including the Qur'an, for its legibility.

muqarnas.name: Muqarnas
muqarnas.summary: A three-dimensional, tiered niche-like decoration in Islamic architecture, likely developed in 11th-century Iraq, used to transition from walls to domes and vaults.

taynal-mosque.name: Taynal Mosque
taynal-mosque.summary: A historic Sunni mosque in Tripoli, Lebanon, on the Abu Ali River, ranked among the city's most important religious monuments after the Mansouri Great Mosque.

ablaq.name: Ablaq
ablaq.summary: Architectural technique of alternating rows of light and dark stone used decoratively in Islamic architecture, possibly derived from earlier Byzantine building methods in the region.

imad-al-din-zengi.name: Imad ad-Din Zengi
imad-al-din-zengi.summary: A Turkoman atabeg of the Seljuk Empire who ruled Mosul, Aleppo, Hama and later Edessa, and founded the Zengid dynasty; he died in 1146.

edessa.name: Edessa
edessa.summary: An ancient city in Upper Mesopotamia (modern Şanlıurfa, Turkey) founded by Seleucus I Nicator, later capital of the Kingdom of Osroene and, during the Crusades, of the County of Edessa.

county-of-edessa.name: County of Edessa
county-of-edessa.summary: A landlocked 12th-century Crusader state in Upper Mesopotamia centered on the city of Edessa; its fall in 1144 was the first major setback for the Crusader states and helped provoke the Second Crusade.

ilkhanate.name: Ilkhanate
ilkhanate.summary: A Mongol khanate established by Hülegü, grandson of Genghis Khan, ruling Iran and neighboring lands from 1259; it converted to Islam under Ghazan and collapsed after ruler Abu Sa'id died in 1335.

amida-mesopotamia.name: Amida
amida-mesopotamia.summary: An ancient walled city in Upper Mesopotamia on the Tigris, on the site of modern Diyarbakır, Turkey.

ayyubid-dynasty.name: Ayyubid dynasty
ayyubid-dynasty.summary: A Sunni Muslim dynasty of Kurdish origin founded by Saladin in 1171, which ruled Egypt and much of Syria until its own Mamluk soldiers overthrew it in 1250.

artuqids.name: Artuqids
artuqids.summary: A Turkish dynasty founded in 1102 that ruled parts of northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia through the 11th to 13th centuries, split into branches at Hasankeyf, Mardin and Harput.

seljuk-dynasty.name: Seljuk dynasty
seljuk-dynasty.summary: The Oghuz Turkic, Sunni Muslim ruling family, also called the House of Seljuk, that founded the Seljuk Empire along with the Sultanates of Kermân and Rum, targets of the First Crusade.

thoros-of-edessa.name: Thoros of Edessa
thoros-of-edessa.summary: An Armenian former Byzantine officer who became ruler of Edessa around 1094, fortifying the city against Seljuk attacks until his death in 1098 during the First Crusade.

numayrid-dynasty.name: Numayrid dynasty
numayrid-dynasty.summary: An Arab dynasty ruling parts of Upper Mesopotamia from 990, controlling cities like Harran and Raqqa until the Seljuk conquest in the late 11th century; emir Mani' ibn Shabib later fortified Harran as his palace.

uqaylid-dynasty.name: Uqaylid dynasty
uqaylid-dynasty.summary: A Shia Arab dynasty that ruled much of Iraq, the Levant, and parts of Anatolia and Iran in the late 10th and 11th centuries, centered on Mosul.

seljuk-empire.name: Seljuk Empire
seljuk-empire.summary: A medieval Turco-Persian empire founded in 1037 by brothers Tughril and Chaghri, stretching from Anatolia to Central Asia, whose 1071 victory at Manzikert weakened Byzantine control there.

upper-mesopotamia.name: Upper Mesopotamia
upper-mesopotamia.summary: The uplands and plain of northwestern Iraq, northeastern Syria and southeastern Turkey, known since the 7th century as al-Jazira, 'the island,' between the Tigris and Euphrates.

matthew-of-edessa.name: Matthew of Edessa
matthew-of-edessa.summary: Armenian abbot and historian (late 11th century–1144) whose chronicle is a key source on the Bagratuni kingdom, the early Crusades, and Byzantine-Arab wars.

steven-runciman.name: Steven Runciman
steven-runciman.summary: An English historian (1903–2000) best known for his three-volume A History of the Crusades, which shaped popular Western views of the Crusades.

hasankeyf.name: Hasankeyf
hasankeyf.summary: A town on the Tigris in Batman Province, Turkey, whose historic town and archaeological sites were flooded by the Ilısu Dam project by 2020.

timurid-empire.name: Timurid Empire
timurid-empire.summary: A Turco-Mongol, Persian-influenced Muslim empire founded by Timur in 1370, dominating Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan and Central Asia into the 15th century.

sultanate-of-rum.name: Sultanate of Rum
sultanate-of-rum.summary: Turco-Persian Muslim state the Seljuk Turks established over conquered Byzantine Anatolia after 1071, considered the beginning of Turkish history in the region.

al-kamil.name: Al-Kamil
al-kamil.summary: Egyptian ruler and fourth Ayyubid sultan of Egypt (c. 1177-1238) who defeated the Fifth Crusade and later ceded West Jerusalem to the Christians during the Sixth Crusade.

maqamat-al-hariri.name: Maqamat al-Hariri
maqamat-al-hariri.summary: Collection of fifty tales written around the late 11th or early 12th century by al-Hariri of Basra, a Seljuk Empire official. Over a hundred manuscripts survive, thirteen of them illustrated.

sebastian-brock.name: Sebastian Brock
sebastian-brock.summary: A British scholar born in 1938, regarded as one of the foremost specialists in Classical Syriac language, literature and Christian cultural history.

barhebraeus.name: Bar Hebraeus
barhebraeus.summary: 13th-century Syriac Christian scholar and maphrian (regional primate) of the Syriac Orthodox Church, known for a universal chronicle and works spanning theology, philosophy, medicine and science.

g-kb-ri.name: Gökböri
g-kb-ri.summary: Leading emir and general under Sultan Saladin and ruler of Erbil (1154–1233), who served both Zengid and Ayyubid rulers and was the first Muslim ruler to publicly celebrate the Prophet Muhammad's birthday.

erbil.name: Erbil
erbil.summary: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, now capital of Iraq's Kurdistan Region, settled since the 5th millennium BC and ruled in turn by Assyrian, Persian, Greek, and other empires.

mawlid.name: Mawlid
mawlid.summary: An annual Islamic festival marking the birthday of the prophet Muhammad, first publicly celebrated by Saladin's deputy Gökböri and later made an official Ottoman holiday.

muhammad.name: Muhammad
muhammad.summary: The founder of Islam, born around 570 CE in Mecca, whom Muslims believe received revelations from God beginning around 610 as the final prophet.

hulegu-khan.name: Hulegu Khan
hulegu-khan.summary: Mongol ruler (c. 1217–1265) and grandson of Genghis Khan who conquered much of West Asia, founded the Ilkhanate in Persia, and destroyed Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid dynasty.

hillah.name: Hillah
hillah.summary: A city in central Iraq on the Euphrates near ancient Babylon, once a major center of Islamic scholarship and later a key administrative city under Ottoman and Mandatory Iraq.

house-of-wisdom.name: House of Wisdom
house-of-wisdom.summary: A major Abbasid-era library and academy in Baghdad, founded under caliphs in the 8th century and turned into a public center of scholarship, destroyed in the Mongol siege of 1258.

harun-al-rashid.name: Harun al-Rashid
harun-al-rashid.summary: Fifth Abbasid caliph, reigning 786 to 809, whose rule is traditionally seen as the start of the Islamic Golden Age; he founded the House of Wisdom library in Baghdad.

islamic-golden-age.name: Islamic Golden Age
islamic-golden-age.summary: A period of cultural flourishing in Islamic history from the 8th to 14th century, beginning with Baghdad's House of Wisdom under Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid and ending with the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

siege-of-baghdad.name: Siege of Baghdad (1258)
siege-of-baghdad.summary: The 1258 Mongol assault on Baghdad led by Hulegu, which killed the Abbasid caliph and hundreds of thousands of residents and is traditionally seen as ending the Islamic Golden Age.

jalayirid-sultanate.name: Jalayirid Sultanate
jalayirid-sultanate.summary: A Mongol dynasty that ruled Iraq and western Iran after the Ilkhanate's breakup in the 1330s, lasting until eliminated by the Qara Qoyunlu in 1432; noted for patronizing Persian art.

ibn-al-mustawfi.name: Ibn al-Mustawfi
ibn-al-mustawfi.summary: A Muslim historian of Erbil (1169–1239), born in its ancient citadel, who wrote on history, literature and language, most notably a four-volume history of Erbil.

ibn-khallikan.name: Ibn Khallikan
ibn-khallikan.summary: A 13th-century Islamic historian (1211–1282) renowned for compiling a celebrated biographical encyclopedia of Muslim scholars, regarded as Islamic history's foremost biographer.

ibn-al-nafis.name: Ibn al-Nafis
ibn-al-nafis.summary: An Arab polymath working in medicine, surgery and philosophy who was the first to describe pulmonary circulation of the blood, pre-dating William Harvey's 1628 work on the subject.

theologus-autodidactus.name: Theologus Autodidactus
theologus-autodidactus.summary: An Arabic novel written by Ibn al-Nafis between 1268 and 1277, considered one of the earliest Arabic novels, blending science fiction, a coming-of-age tale, and a desert island story.

ismail-al-jazari.name: al-Jazari
ismail-al-jazari.summary: Polymath and mechanical engineer in Mesopotamia (1136-1206) who wrote a 1206 book describing 50 mechanical devices, including the famous elephant clock, earning him the title 'father of robotics'.

elephant-clock.name: Elephant clock
elephant-clock.summary: A model water clock invented by medieval Islamic engineer Ismail al-Jazari, described in his 1206 book on mechanical devices.

ibn-al-haytham.name: Ibn al-Haytham
ibn-al-haytham.summary: A mathematician, astronomer and physicist of the Islamic Golden Age from Iraq (c. 965–1040), known as 'the father of modern optics' and frequently cited by later Scientific Revolution figures like Galileo and Kepler.

book-of-optics.name: Book of Optics
book-of-optics.summary: A seven-volume treatise on optics by the medieval scholar Ibn al-Haytham (965–c.1040), arguing that vision works because light enters the eye and pioneering early use of the scientific method.

ibn-al-shatir.name: Ibn al-Shatir
ibn-al-shatir.summary: An Arab astronomer, mathematician and engineer (1304–1375) who worked as timekeeper at Damascus's Umayyad Mosque and built a sundial for its minaret in 1371–72.

umayyad-mosque.name: Umayyad Mosque
umayyad-mosque.summary: Great Mosque of Damascus, one of the oldest and largest mosques in the world, built on a site used for worship since the Iron Age; tradition holds it contains the head of John the Baptist.

nur-al-din-bimaristan.name: Nur al-Din Bimaristan
nur-al-din-bimaristan.summary: A medieval hospital in Damascus, built in 1154 for the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din and later extended, now home to a museum of medicine.

galen.name: Galen
galen.summary: A Roman-era Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher (129–c.216 CE) whose anatomical writings, shaped by the four-humors theory, dominated Western medicine for over 1,300 years.

ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
ptolemy.summary: A Greco-Roman scholar of the 2nd century AD who wrote influential works on astronomy, geography and astrology; his geocentric model of the universe, promoted by the Catholic Church, was studied for over a thousand years.

almagest.name: Almagest
almagest.summary: Ptolemy's 2nd-century astronomical treatise that established the geocentric model of the universe, accepted for over 1,200 years.

equant.name: Equant
equant.summary: A mathematical concept devised by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD to explain the varying speed of planets while preserving the idea of uniform circular motion.

al-adudi-hospital.name: Al-Adudi Hospital
al-adudi-hospital.summary: A hospital in medieval Baghdad, built under the Buyid ruler Adud al-Dawla, considered one of the most innovative institutions of its time for practicing and teaching medicine.

candle-clock.name: Candle clock
candle-clock.summary: A thin candle marked at even intervals so that, as it burned down, it showed how much time had passed, once used to tell time indoors or at night.

abbasid-caliphate.name: Abbasid Caliphate
abbasid-caliphate.summary: The third Islamic caliphate, ruling from 750 to 1258 with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time, known for ushering in the Islamic Golden Age of science and culture.

al-musta-sim.name: al-Musta'sim
al-musta-sim.summary: The 37th and last Abbasid caliph, holding the title from 1242 until his death in 1258, when Baghdad fell to the Mongols and the dynasty ended.

fatimid-caliphate.name: Fatimid Caliphate
fatimid-caliphate.summary: An Isma'ili Shia caliphate ruling North Africa and West Asia from the 10th to 12th centuries CE, claiming descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, with Egypt as its eventual centre.

battle-of-hattin.name: Battle of Hattin
battle-of-hattin.summary: A decisive 1187 battle in which Saladin's forces destroyed the Crusader armies of the Levant, leading to the recapture of Jerusalem and prompting the Third Crusade.

crusader-states.name: Crusader states
crusader-states.summary: Four Catholic states set up in the Levant and southeastern Anatolia between 1098 and 1291 after the First Crusade, including the Kingdom of Jerusalem, also called Outremer.

atabeg.name: Atabeg
atabeg.summary: Hereditary Turkic noble title for a governor subordinate to a monarch, originally tasked with raising the crown prince; first used by the Seljuks and later in the Kingdom of Georgia.

nur-al-din-arslan-shah-i.name: Nur al-Din Arslan Shah I
nur-al-din-arslan-shah-i.summary: Zengid emir of Mosul from 1193 to 1211, who fought and made truces with the Ayyubids and relied on his commander Badr al-Din Lu'lu' as his health declined.

badr-al-din-lu-lu.name: Badr al-Din Lu'lu'
badr-al-din-lu-lu.summary: Successor to the Zengid emirs of Mosul who governed the city from 1234 to 1259, rising from enslaved origins to found the short-lived Lu'lu'id dynasty.

ghilman.name: Ghilman
ghilman.summary: Slave-soldiers or mercenaries used across Islamic armies from the 9th to 19th centuries, a practice historians note was rare outside the Islamic world.

harran.name: Harran
harran.summary: Ancient city in Upper Mesopotamia, founded between the 25th and 20th centuries BC, a major religious centre devoted to the moon god Sin and site of the 53 BC Battle of Carrhae.

marwanid-dynasty-diyar-bakr.name: Marwanid dynasty
marwanid-dynasty-diyar-bakr.summary: Kurdish Sunni Muslim dynasty (983–1085) that ruled the Diyar Bakr region of Upper Mesopotamia, centered on the city of Mayyafariqin.

nasr-al-dawla-ahmad-ibn-marwan.name: Nasr al-Dawla
nasr-al-dawla-ahmad-ibn-marwan.summary: Ruler of the Marwanid Emirate from 1011 to 1061, regarded as guardian of the Islamic frontier and expected to campaign against Christian territories.

al-hakim-bi-amr-allah.name: Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah
al-hakim-bi-amr-allah.summary: Sixth Fatimid caliph and sixteenth Ismaili imam (985-1021), a deeply controversial ruler seen by some as a tyrant and by others as an ideal, divinely ordained sovereign.

basil-ii.name: Basil II
basil-ii.summary: Byzantine emperor from 976 to 1025, nicknamed the Bulgar Slayer for conquering the First Bulgarian Empire; his 49-year reign was the longest of any Roman emperor.

george-maniakes.name: George Maniakes
george-maniakes.summary: Byzantine army general of the 11th century, reputed to be extremely tall, who served as catepan (governor) of Italy in 1042.

al-adil-i.name: Al-Adil I
al-adil-i.summary: Fourth Sultan of Egypt and Syria (1145-1218) and brother of Saladin, a skilled administrator and general who helped found the Ayyubid dynasty.

sinjar.name: Sinjar
sinjar.summary: A town near the Sinjar Mountains in northern Iraq's Nineveh Governorate, with a population that is predominantly Yazidi.

syriac-christianity.name: Syriac Christianity
syriac-christianity.summary: A branch of Eastern Christianity expressed in the Classical Syriac language, one of Early Christianity's three major literary languages alongside Greek and Latin.

syriac-renaissance.name: Syriac Renaissance
syriac-renaissance.summary: A modern term for a revival of Syriac literary and scholarly culture from roughly the 11th to 13th centuries, under Islamic and Mongol rule.

nur-al-din-zengi.name: Nur al-Din Zengi
nur-al-din-zengi.summary: A Turkoman ruler of the Zengid dynasty who reigned from 1146 to 1174 and emphasized Arab rather than Turkish or Persian titles.

mor-mattai-monastery.name: Mor Mattai Monastery
mor-mattai-monastery.summary: A Syriac Orthodox monastery on Mount Alfaf near Mosul in northern Iraq, one of the oldest Christian monasteries in existence, known for its library of Syriac manuscripts.

al-basasiri.name: Al-Basasiri
al-basasiri.summary: A Turkoman military commander who switched allegiance to the Fatimid Caliphate and conquered Baghdad in 1058, ruling it for nearly a year before dying in 1059.

al-qa-im.name: al-Qa'im
al-qa-im.summary: Abbasid caliph at Baghdad from 1031 to 1075, son of al-Qadir.

al-muqtadi.name: al-Muqtadi
al-muqtadi.summary: Abbasid caliph in Baghdad from 1075 to 1094, born in 1056, who succeeded his grandfather al-Qa'im on the throne.

hama.name: Hama
hama.summary: A city on the Orontes River in west-central Syria, known for its historic water-wheels (norias) and cheesemaking tradition.

abulfeda.name: Abu al-Fida
abulfeda.summary: Kurdish geographer, historian, Ayyubid prince and governor of Hama under Mamluk rule (1273–1331).

al-afdal-muhammad.name: Al-Afdal Muhammad
al-afdal-muhammad.summary: Last Ayyubid governor of Hama in Syria, reigning 1332-1341, son of the geographer Abu'l-Fida, deposed by the Mamluks.

mamluk.name: Mamluks
mamluk.summary: Non-Arab enslaved soldiers, often of Turkic or Circassian origin, who converted to Islam and trained for war before being freed to serve as an elite military and political class in Egypt for nearly 1,000 years.

ghulam.name: Ghulam
ghulam.summary: An Arabic word for servant or youth, also used for slave-soldiers in the Abbasid, Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires.

sin-mythology.name: Sin (Nanna)
sin-mythology.summary: Mesopotamian god of the moon, also called Nanna, associated with cattle herding, the crescent symbol, and sometimes seen as a judge of the dead.

neoplatonism.name: Neoplatonism
neoplatonism.summary: A version of Platonic philosophy emerging in the 3rd century AD, holding that reality derives from a single principle, 'the One,' and influencing later Christian, Jewish and Muslim thought.

hermeticism.name: Hermeticism
hermeticism.summary: A philosophical and religious tradition based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, produced between about 300 BCE and 1200 CE.

al-andalus.name: Al-Andalus
al-andalus.summary: The Muslim-ruled territories of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, which at their height covered all of Spain and Portugal, with Córdoba becoming a leading cultural and scientific center.

sufi-lodge.name: Khanqah
sufi-lodge.summary: A building for gatherings of a Sufi brotherhood, used for spiritual practice and religious education, sometimes state-sponsored and attached to hospitals or kitchens.

ibn-jubayr.name: Ibn Jubayr
ibn-jubayr.summary: An Andalusian geographer, traveller and poet (1145–1217) whose chronicle of his 1183–1185 pilgrimage to Mecca describes Saladin's domains and Christian Sicily's mixed culture.

sabians.name: Sabians
sabians.summary: A religious group named in the Quran whose true identity is uncertain; the name was later claimed by groups such as the star-worshipping Sabians of Harran.

hilal-al-sabi.name: Hilal ibn al-Muhassin
hilal-al-sabi.summary: Hilal ibn al-Muhassin: A historian, bureaucrat and writer (969-1056) born into a family of Sabian officials, who converted to Islam around 1012 and later directed the chancery under a Buyid vizier.

th-bit-ibn-qurra.name: Thābit ibn Qurra
th-bit-ibn-qurra.summary: Pagan Sabian scholar (826 or 836–901) active in Abbasid Baghdad who made major discoveries in mathematics, astronomy and medicine.

adab-islam.name: adab
adab-islam.summary: Islamic code of etiquette covering manners, decorum and proper behaviour in daily life, reflecting personal refinement and social standing.

yazidism.name: Yazidism
yazidism.summary: A monotheistic Kurdish ethnic religion shaped by pre-Islamic Kurdish belief and Sufi teachings, centered on one God and seven angels led by the Peacock Angel.

sheikh-adi-ibn-musafir.name: Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir
sheikh-adi-ibn-musafir.summary: A 12th-century mystic and theologian (1072/1078–1162) regarded as the central saint and reformer of the Yazidi religion, whose tomb at Lalish is Yazidism's holiest site.

lalish.name: Lalish
lalish.summary: The holiest temple of the Yazidis, a mountain valley in northern Iraq holding the tomb of Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir, a central figure of the Yazidi faith.

shinar.name: Shinar
shinar.summary: The name used in the Hebrew Bible for the southern region of Mesopotamia, traditionally the setting of the Tower of Babel story.

bahir.name: Bahir
bahir.summary: An anonymous 12th-century Jewish mystical text, one of the earliest works of Kabbalah, traditionally but wrongly attributed to a 1st-century rabbi.

book-of-the-bee.name: Book of the Bee
book-of-the-bee.summary: A Syriac compilation of biblical stories and theology written around 1222 by Solomon of Akhlat, Bishop of Basra, covering topics from creation to the resurrection.

dante-alighieri.name: Dante Alighieri
dante-alighieri.summary: Italian poet and philosopher (c. 1265–1321) famed for the Divine Comedy, and a pioneer of writing in vernacular Tuscan rather than Latin.

adam.name: Adam
adam.summary: First human named in the Bible; in Christian belief, his eating from the tree of knowledge in the Garden of Eden introduced sin and death into the world; also a key figure in Judaism, Islam and other faiths.

de-vulgari-eloquentia.name: De vulgari eloquentia
de-vulgari-eloquentia.summary: An unfinished Latin essay written by Dante Alighieri around 1302 to 1305, arguing that vernacular languages deserved the same dignity as Latin.

divine-comedy.name: Divine Comedy
divine-comedy.summary: Narrative poem by Dante Alighieri (c. 1308-1321) describing a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Heaven, considered a pre-eminent work of Italian and Western literature.

giovanni-villani.name: Giovanni Villani
giovanni-villani.summary: A Florentine banker and official (c. 1276/1280–1348) who wrote the Nuova Cronica, a year-by-year chronicle of Florence and Europe, notable for its early use of statistics in history.

gesta-hunnorum-et-hungarorum.name: Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum
gesta-hunnorum-et-hungarorum.summary: Medieval Latin chronicle written around 1282–1285, mainly by Simon of Kéza, blending Hunnish legend with the early history of the Kingdom of Hungary.

shem.name: Shem
shem.summary: A son of Noah in the Bible, regarded in Jewish, Christian and Islamic tradition as ancestor of various Near Eastern peoples.

ham-genesis.name: Ham
ham-genesis.summary: According to the Book of Genesis, a son of Noah whose descendants were later associated with the peopling of Africa, including Egypt.

japheth.name: Japheth
japheth.summary: One of Noah's three sons in the Book of Genesis, later named ancestor of peoples of the Aegean, Anatolia, Caucasus and Greece, and seen in medieval Europe as forefather of Europeans.

el-deity.name: El
el-deity.summary: A Northwest Semitic word for 'god', and the name of the supreme deity of ancient Canaanite religion, described as father of the gods and creator of humanity.
